utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Russo, the Chamber was informed you would like to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President, and good morning. Two issues. Number one, I have two documents that I intend to use with the witness, which we've just put together this morning. I've provided hard copies to the Trial Chamber and to Defence counsel. We're attempting to put those into e-court right now. If not, we may use them via Sanction. However, I do also have hard copies for the witness, but I didn't want there to be any confusion when I started using these documents. The second issue relates to the CD of The Blue Book that we received yesterday. I'm not sure if this is an oversight, but the CD we received does not contain the organigrams which are found within the book. The organigrams are actually fold-out pages in the physical book, itself, but those organigrams are not contained on the CD that we received. I don't know if we can receive those separately or what the issue is there, but I wanted to advise the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the blue books -- The Blue Book comes from the Markac Defence. Mr. Mikulicic, any comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, Your Honour, I'm not aware of what is on CD or what is not on CD. We just copied the CD that we received with The Blue Book. So the organigrams that my learned colleague is talking about is composed within The Blue Book, so there's the opportunity to scan them and then to make a copy of it. So that's all I can say. I have no explanation whether they are included in the CD or they are not included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it that can be scanned. However, another issue arose, more or less, in relation to these organigrams, these diagrams. Mr. Russo, Mr. Mikulicic gave you what he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President, if that's -- I just wasn't sure if they are not included by accident. But if that's the form in which he received them, we don't have any issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The other matter is the use of certain documents which are provided in hard copy to the Chamber, apparently do not raise any further need for submissions. Since the witness is not in, I'd briefly like to deal with another matter. In relation to the statement of Witness AG-10, which is a 92 bis statement, some time was left to the Gotovina Defence to ask for protective measures. We have not received any request until now. Mr. Misetic, does that mean that there will be no request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. As I understand it -- just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand it, we will make the formal motion because the witness, in his 92 bis declaration, asked for them. I have not been in contact with the witness to ask for his reasons, but there is a request from the witness, himself, for these measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that, of course, has to be formalised in one way or the other. We can't go to the witness and ask him what the reasons were. How much time would you need for that, because the matter is pending already -- no, it's pending since 16th of September. The decision was filed in which the statement was admitted into evidence, and in that same decision we have invited the Gotovina Defence to request protective measures within seven days, and that was 23rd or the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I apologise for that. I hope to get you an answer today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we at least -- whatever the outcome is here, not any later than the 28th. That is next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic. First of all, our apologies for inviting you into the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then to ask you to leave again. Our apologies for that. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday, at the beginning of your testimony, still binds you. And Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, again, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning your attention back to paragraph 5.1.7 of your report, and we left off on this topic yesterday, I wanted to get a more specific explanation from you. Back when the 1994 rules were promulgated, was there a concern about the military police conducting investigations of the army while under the command of HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons why the military police was withdrawn from the system of the military forces and the subordination of the military forces. Any punishable act which constituted a crime would have been processed, and we know that a commander can influence the military police if that military police is under that commander, when it comes to prosecuting certain acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kovacevic. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, in section 0.2.1 of your report, you indicate that your main objective is to present your report in a neutral and objective manner. Now, you've made a number of public statements regarding this case which I would like to take a look at, at this moment, and which I'm going to suggest to you demonstrate that, in fact, you're neither neutral nor objective with respect to this case. If we could begin, please, with 65 ter 7414. Mr. Kovacevic, the article which is now on the screen is an article which purports to be written by you concerning the Croatian government's response to the indictments in this case. It's published on the 12th of April, 2007. Do you recall this article?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write the article. It must have been a journalist. And my report is professional and doesn't contain either political or my personal views. At that time, I was an MP in the Croatian Parliament, which means that I was also a politician. However, it is true that I urged the government to establish the Croatian Memorial Centre as a body that would collect documents from the homeland war and provide it to anybody who might be interested in it, which means that you also would have had an easier job if this had been done earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can move to the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you can see, at the end of the article, it's, in fact, attributed as being signed by you. Is it your position that you did not write this article?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Please bear with me. I'd like to look at the first part of the article. I don't know if this is the column that I published or whether this is an article written by a journalist, because I also at one point wrote columns for newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move back to the first page of the document and we'll have you just take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you could. Thank you. Yes, this is a column that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the second paragraph of the article, if we could focus on that, you write: "The indictments are not only directed against the generals, but also against Croatia." Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I will put it to you that you drafted the expert report that you submitted not for the purpose of providing a neutral and objective opinion, but, in fact, to undermine the indictments which you perceived to be an attack upon Croatia, itself. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I'm a professional. These are political statements which supported my political struggle in the Parliament. And as my report goes, I drafted it as a professional, familiar with the regulations, and I always make a distinction between my political and personal views and my professional views. When I write a report, I base the report on my professional views, which you can easily conclude, yourself, when you read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of the article, the second sentence, you write: "The Croatian Party of Rights (HSP) has issued warnings and drawn the government's attention to the commitment to take a series of legal, political, and diplomatic measures to bring down the monstrous Hague indictments." Now, the Croatian Party of Rights, the HSPs, is your political party; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Former -- that's my former political party. Since 2008, I have not been a member of that party because I did not agree with the non-democratic decision-making process in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, and my apologies for that. And I'll suggest to you, Mr. Kovacevic, that your report and your testimony here today are, in fact, a continuation of these legal, political, and diplomatic measures to bring down the indictments. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report is a professional report based on the regulations that I drafted, and in my professional report there is not a single political statement. It doesn't contain any of my personal views vis-a-vis anything. As I've already told you, I am a professional when it comes to drafting such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at the third paragraph, Mr. Kovacevic, you write: "We expressed this viewpoint several times, both in our written initiatives and during Parliament debates, the purpose of which was to commit the government to take legal, diplomatic, political, and other measures. Does the public know that the archive and registry material created in the homeland war has not been put in order to this day, for the purpose of promoting the truth about the homeland war, what all the obstacles are that were put before the indicted generals before they could get the documents they sought, and that the generals were forced to buy the necessary documents for their defence on the black market." Mr. Kovacevic, I want to talk about the generals purchasing documents for their defence on the black market. Now, first, can you tell us what exactly this black market is and how it works.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never operated on the black market. I'm a lawyer. However, as an MP in the Croatian Parliament, I learned that General Praljak, for example, was forced to buy the document that he was missing on the black market because the state had not established a documentation centre, it had not put in order all the documents, which every state is obliged to do under the law on archives. Every state has to have documentation in place. And I am only happy that I finally succeeded in my initiative. You know that every state works in the same way. They have political and legal measures in place, and the legal thing that I asked for was for Croatia to become the friend of The Hague Tribunal, and that is helping the Tribunal, the government, and the fact that the Government of Croatia is the amicus of the Tribunal. The government puts in place political and legal measures, and the opposition is the one that pin-points all the government's shortcomings and omissions in order to gain popularity with the general public. Every opposition in every corner of the world acts the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Mr. Kovacevic, but I'd like to focus, in particular, about the black market. Now, you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I had some difficulties in understanding at least one line of that last answer. You said: "They have political and legal measures in place, and the legal thing that I asked for was for Croatia to become the friend of The Hague Tribunal, and that is helping the Tribunal, the government, and the fact that the Government of Croatia is the amicus of the Tribunal." Now, what's -- you said "the legal thing." What's exactly "the legal thing," and does that mean that you positively appreciate the cooperation by the Croatian Government with this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to the cooperation, it can be evaluated by the Tribunal, itself. On several occasions, this cooperation has been evaluated positively. And as far as legal measures are concerned, the measure in question is the one according to which a state may be asked for the status of an amicus of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked whether you positively appreciated that, because that seems, although not very clear to me, part --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course I see it as a positive development. This cooperation is in keeping with the constitutional law, and it is a positive development, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, in the article you write: "... a clumsy and forced attempt to obtain the status of the Tribunal's friend." That doesn't sound very much positive, as far as your appreciation is concerned, but correct me when I understand this wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying here is that the legal measures that the government put in place was not something that was done in due course and in keeping with the Rules of the work of the Tribunal, its Statute, and other documents. It was a belated attempt. The council that was supposed to deal with the matters and Croatia becoming a friend of the Tribunal, was established rather late, and Croatia failed in putting things in place on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from what I understand from the article - but please, again, correct me when I'm reading it wrongly - at the expense of the defence of accused persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no documentation and archives in order, in different collections, obviously this is at the expense of the Defence, because the Defence teams cannot obtain documents that they need and that they deem necessary for their case, and the state is the one that is to blame for that. The archives are still being put in order. It was only in 2005 when the documentation centre was formally established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we're going to come back to the issue of cooperation with the Tribunal, but I want to concentrate for the moment on the black market. Now, you indicated that you had heard that General Praljak had to obtain documents on the black market. Now, I'd like to learn, first of all, how you came by that information and the full content of the information you came upon regarding this black market.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could come across such information in the media. I don't know by which channels I actually received that. Maybe there was a letter of someone who wrote things like that. In any case, I simply used that to further my argument to show that there is yet another reason to establish the documentation memorial centre that I was insisting upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you come across any information that either Generals Gotovina, Cermak, or Markac have received documents from the black market?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are you in a position to positively confirm that any of the documentation you reviewed in your analysis was not obtained off this black market?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the documents I reviewed bear either the stamp of the Prosecution, or they have already been made exhibits, or they can be found on the Defence list of General Cermak for tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I move for the admission of 65 ter 7414.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2635.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2635 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could now please have 65 ter 7412.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, what you see on your screen is an article in the same publication, dated 1 October 2007, regarding efforts by you and your political party to bring a referendum on discontinuing cooperation with the ICTY. Are you familiar with this article?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an article about the initiative to launch a referendum on any further cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. This was part of my political activities as an MP and, at the time, member of the HSP Party. This was a result of the great dissatisfaction across Croatia concerning the judgement that was pronounced to the Vukovar Three. This is nothing to do with my expert report. My expert report is a professional piece of work which does not contain any of my personal or political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The article begins: "Today we will surpass the number of 100.000 signatures for the petition to hold a referendum about the further cooperation with The Hague. But to make the petition legally binding, we need 400.000, says HSP representative Pero Kovacevic. "After the verdict against the war criminals Veselin Sljivancanin, Miroslav Radic, and Mile Mrksic, the cessation of cooperation with The Hague and the return of the Croatian generals in order to be tried in Croatia is the only option left after years of Croatia's 'servile strategy' toward the Court in The Hague, claims Kovacevic in an interview for Index." Now, Mr. Kovacevic, can you explain why you believed terminating cooperation between Croatia and this Tribunal, and trying the generals in Croatia, is an appropriate response to a verdict in an unrelated case?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was undertaken by my former party in 2007, in October, during the election campaign for the Parliament in Croatia. These are purely political activities by the party, and I was a member of that party at the time. I participated in those political activities. But this has absolutely nothing to do with the expert report I produced. This is in the sphere of my political activity alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, the truth is that you wanted to end cooperation between Croatia and this Tribunal so that Croatia would not have to hand over evidence which could establish the allegations in this indictment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. This is a political statement. Croatia is a member state of the UN. This Tribunal was created by virtue of a UN Security Council resolution. Croatia is a full member. On behalf of the Croatian government, I did actually participate in the drafting of a letter putting forth the initiative to establish this Court in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm going to suggest to you that contrary to the distinction you are attempting to draw between your political -- or your actions as a politician and your work as an expert in this case, that, in fact, your failed attempts to dissolve official cooperation between the Government of Croatia and this Tribunal, and indeed the report and the testimony you're giving here today, are simply part of the legal, political, diplomatic, and other measures which you say your party has pursued, and I'm suggesting to you that those are pursued to undermine the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that is incorrect. As I have already said, I am no longer a member of the Croatian Party of Rights. Everyone within the domain of his or her profession should distinguish between his or her political and professional activities. This expert report is professional. If a baker says something that you find politically incorrect, you're not going to say that his bread is bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Kovacevic. Mr. President, I'd move for the admission of 65 ter 7412.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2636.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2636 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have a look at one more article. That is 65 ter 7413.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And before we move to this, let me just ask you a separate question, Mr. Kovacevic. As a former member of Parliament, can you explain to this Trial Chamber what happens if a parliamentary member lies to the Parliament? Are there official sanctions for that? Tell us what happens in that event.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For everything uttered in the Parliament, such an MP enjoys immunity, according to the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the Rules of Procedure of the Croatian Parliament. A parliament is a political forum. That's a clear thing. It goes without saying. Any opposition parliamentary party is striving to point out the shortcomings and use any possible opportunity to attack those currently in power. Congressmen and senators are politicians, much as parliamentarians, but one, as I said, should always distinguish between one's professional and political activity, and in such situations, it cannot happen that one mixes up the two things, the political and professional sphere. You also know that there were statements of Sir Geoffrey Nice and the former spokeswoman of the Prosecution, and the Prosecutor, herself, and such statements frequently contained political points. This is simply a matter of policy. But a legal domain is one, the professional another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. Looking at the article on the screen, this is an article dated 26 February 2008. I'm sorry, if we could actually move to the next page in both B/C/S and English. This article is dated the 26th of February, 2008, regarding the indictment in this case. If we could actually move to page 3 in the English and stay on page 2 in the B/C/S, and focus on the bottom on the page of B/C/S. And towards the bottom of the page in English, where it begins: "Kovacevic ..." Mr. Kovacevic, the following is attributed to you in this article: "Pero Kovacevic of HSPs -- HSP's Croatian Party of Rights, emphasizes that so far the indictment has been generalised, so the OTP is tidying it up now. However, he considers this way a half-crazy attempt of the OTP to justify itself. They want to accuse Markac, Cermak, and Gotovina of absolutely everything."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't find this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have it on my screen, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we can move up a bit in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm using my e-court screen rather than the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies. I directed the Registrar to the wrong portion of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: "They want to accuse Markac, Cermak, and Gotovina of absolutely everything. Even of something that does not exist in the national legislature. You cannot accuse the three of them of something for which some civilians or servicemen should be responsible, emphasizes Kovacevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of our clients, if we could turn the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And my apologies. "The Defence, given that it is the real one, Kovacevic believes, does not have a hard task because the defendants cannot be proven 'the interference in someone else's work.' "In a part of the investigation, none of these three men has anything to do with anything. They could not do the job of military and civil police. Only if they had done that, only then they would have done something illegal, emphasizes Kovacevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you recall making these statements at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an authorised statement. Perhaps if I received a phone call, I don't know whether I said so word for word. I never verified it. Secondly, this is yet another political statement. I have already told you that I frequently gave political statements as a Croatian MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just to be clear, although you indicate that it's not an authorised statement, do these statements which are attributed to you accurately reflect your beliefs at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're asking me one thing, and I'm talking about the statements which are of political nature. I hope you understand. We are here today to discuss my report, which is a professional one. This is all the difference. There is an important difference between you, as a person, giving a political statement and you, as a professional, producing an expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, may I invite you to answer the questions, even though you consider that we are limited to discussing your report. The Prosecution is entitled to draw the attention of the Chamber to public statements you made earlier. So the last question, which you have not answered yet, is whether this publication reflects, although as you said, political views you held at the time it was published or whether it does not reflect your views at the time. Again, I do understand political views, or at least views expressed in a political environment, in a political context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the policy of my former party. And as a party official, I was tasked with stating those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you disagreed with that, would you have asked your party to ask someone else to express some things you disagreed with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It just so happened that I left the party after that. It wasn't just this situation, but there was several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said, That was the view of my party. Did you disagree with it? You disagreed with what you were asked to tell the public on behalf of the party; is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you should understand it that way. As a lawyer, supporting the rule of law, I was in favour with the constitutional law on cooperation between Croatia and the ICTY. The government needs to abide by that law. We are also bound by the Security Council resolution as a UN member. We have obligations that we have to implement as a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but these last statements are not about cooperation, are they? They are about whether the indictment -- let me just check again. There's nothing about cooperation in the last portion that was put to you. It's just about your criticism on the indictment and that it could never be proven, which is -- has got nothing to do with a duty to cooperate, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd say yes and no, depending on your angle, but it's a simple matter, really. This is a political statement, and the indictment was being amended at the time, and I'm not even sure it's final yet. If something is being amended in the process, it must mean that there was something missing. In any case, this is a political statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's try to get an answer to the questions that are put to you. You say, I disagree with what I was supposed to say on behalf of the party. And then you explained that you left the party and that you, as a lawyer, couldn't support anything else than cooperation, which is a duty for the state of Croatia. Now, none of these statements, at least this one, deals with cooperation. It deals with your assessments of whether the indictment can be proven, whether it's a good or a bad indictment, whether these three men has anything to do with anything. It is a statement which has got nothing to do with the duty of Croatia to cooperate with the Tribunal. It's just your personal assessment of whether this indictment is a good one, whether it can be proven or not, and whether the accused have anything to do with what is found in the indictment, and who would be responsible. That's -- for me, it's difficult to understand why you say, I disagree with that because I find that we have to cooperate, as a state, with the Tribunal. So, therefore, could you try to explain to me how I have to understand your last answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the part concerning the indictment, this was a political statement of mine at the time, based on what was being broached in the Croatian media as to the way the indictment was put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let me then stop you there. You said, This is what I had to say on behalf of the party. I asked you whether you disagreed or not, whether this was your, though, political view at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My political view of the indictment was the way I stated here. It was widely believed that it was incomplete. I could not address the legal side of it because I did not have all the required information. I could only comment on what one could come across in the headings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in one of your earlier answers, you said you disagreed, and you explained why. And now, two or three questions later, you say, No, that was my political view at the time. I'm a bit confused about hearing one answer at one moment. And I'm referring the parties to page 19 -- my question starting on page 18, line 25, and the answer starting on page 19, line 4, and the answer you just gave. If you want to further explain, please do so, and otherwise I'll ask Mr. Russo to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, we misunderstand each other. The first part of the answer had to do with the suspension of cooperation with The Hague Tribunal in relation to the petition and referendum. As a lawyer, I said that it was a clear thing that Croatia needs to fulfill its obligations which it had undertaken. The latter part concerns the Croatian media of -- and their reports of the indictment and its process of amending. These were two separate things, and I don't think they contradict each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, you draw a distinction between the statements you made in this article and the opinions expressed in your report. However, the last part of this article which I read, which is -- I'll quote again: "In a part of the investigation, none of these three men has anything to do with anything, they could not do the job of military and civil police. Only if they had done that, only then they would have done something illegal ..." Now, aren't these the same opinions that are expressed in your report, specifically that addressing crime was not the responsibility of the HV commanders; that it was the responsibility of the military and civil police? Aren't those the same opinions?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part, I said something that belonged in the professional domain, since I drafted the Law on Defence, the Law on the Service in the Armed Forces, as well as different regulations about the structure of the military police and the police. I spoke in legal terms, in terms of subordination and the duties of superiors, as well as the obligations that the two types of police had under the Croatian legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you made these statements and expressed those opinions in February of 2008, which is before the trial in this matter began, before the Prosecution had presented any evidence in support of its indictment. And I'll suggest to you that your statements here indicate that you formed your opinions well before taking a neutral and objective look at the evidence which has been provided. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no. Political activity is one thing, a professional report is another thing; and there's always a difference there, a very important difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move for the admission of 65 ter 7413.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2637.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, are you familiar with Mr. Franjo Feldi?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've known him since 1991, when he joined the Croatian Army sometime in the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you aware of Mr. Feldi's position on the Cermak Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you follow the testimony of Mr. Feldi over the course of the last few days?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched some short parts of it on Tuesday, on the first day, and after that I didn't watch the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you otherwise learn of the general substance of the testimony, other than what you watched on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed some reports on the internet conveyed by the HINA agency regarding the military police which was also part of the testimony. It was a very short report by the Croatian news agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, did you work at all with Mr. Feldi in the preparation of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My expert report was done independently, I did it on my own. Mr. Kay gave me instructions as to what content I should deal with and how many pages I should produce. I was given a brief as to what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did you and Mr. Feldi assist each other in any way in the preparation of your respective reports?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My report is a legal expert -- expertise, and General Feldi is a soldier, and there is a significant difference in the way the two of us may have approached an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Feldi -- I'm sorry. Mr. Kovacevic, I'd like to show you a comparison of some documents in your report and in Mr. Feldi's report. Mr. President, we'd like to do this via Sanction. We're going to show the comparison chart which has been provided to the Chamber and the parties. This is 65 ter 7415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second, please. I said one moment. Mr. Russo, you saw that the Chamber was -- that the Judges were consulting. The Chamber would prefer you first to explore how portions were produced by Mr. Kovacevic before we start comparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the material should be returned to Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, there are a number of organigrams in your expert report. I'd like to know where you got those.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: As I was drafting my report, and as I went through the chapters, I left some room in the first draft of the report, after I'd spoken with Mr. Kay, I left some room for the schematic illustrations of what I dealt with in the chapter. I took the regulations, and you know how schematic illustrations are done. It's very easy. And then Mr. Kay told me that those already existed, that they had already been produced and exist as evidence before this Trial Chamber. They represented the military police, the organisation of the Police Administration of Knin District, the Police Administration of Zadar and Knin, and a few others. I believe that whatever I proposed to do, Mr. Kay told me that there is no need because they already existed, they were in evidence before the Court, and he told me that his support team would provide me with all the necessary graphic illustrations for my report. I believe that the schematic regarding the organisation of the MUP and the map did not exist. I wanted to include the map to show what was covered by the Police Administration of Knin District and what was covered by the Knin Military District. I wanted to have a clear illustration of that. I made most of my schematics by hand. I drew them and showed them to Mr. Kay, who then told me that most of them already exist and have already been put in evidence before this Court. We can go through the schematics one by one and explain each of them in turn. But I can come up with any sort of schematic you want me to. Just give me the parameters, and I will produce one immediately here for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I was under the impression that your report was drafted entirely independently by you. Are you telling me that you received specific documentation from Mr. Kay to include in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it very loud and clear. I hand-drew the schematics that I needed, the Police Administration of Knin District, the Police Administration of Zadar and Knin, the organisation of the military police. I drafted those, and they had to be perfected. And when I told Mr. Kay what would be inserted in the blank spaces, I wanted to show that Knin belonged to the Police Administration of Zadar and Knin, for example, he told me, There is no need, the schematics already exist, they were already drawn by professionals, and they have been tendered into evidence. There's no difference whatsoever with what I proposed, as drawn by my own hand, and what Mr. Kay's team had prepared for this case. There is no difference in the content of the schematics. If there were any differences, then we could be talking about me copying somebody else's work. But there is no difference because the schematics of the MUP are all based on the work of the MUP since February 1995. It is very simple to produce a schematic of any kind. You take a piece of regulation, you look at the organisation, and you transform it into a schematic, and a schematic is a good way to illustrate things which can make even your life easier, if you want to understand what is going on, and especially when it comes to the penal part of the police work, because the police of the Knin District did not have jurisdiction over crime investigation matters. That was part of the administration of Zadar and Knin police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kovacevic. My time is a bit limited, so I didn't ask you about the substance of any particular relationship. I'm trying to understand the process by which these organigrams ended up in your report, and I want to be clear. You're telling me that you drew schematics on your own, showed them to Mr. Kay, Mr. Kay told you that the exact content of these schematics had already been introduced into evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. My schematics were drawn by hand, the boxes were all drawn by hand, and what he proposed to produce was something that had already been admitted into evidence. And he told me, I am going to give you those to save you the trouble of having to draw the schematics in an electronic form, because my schematics, what I proposed to Mr. Kay, had been drawn by my own hand. It had not been done on a laptop, like the text was. My schematics were on pieces of paper, hand-drawn by me. I showed them to Mr. Kay, who then told me, We already have those, they have already been admitted into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: How exactly did this happen? I want to be clear about this. You handed to Mr. Kay hand-drawn schematics. Did he have with him already the organigrams to compare it with to say that they were identical, or did he know immediately, by looking at them, that they were identical?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you how the conversation went. He read the chapters that I drafted professionally, and then I told him, Here, where you see a blank space, I propose to include a schematic that I already have hand-drawn. Mr. Kay asked me what the schematic is going to illustrate. My draft was in Croatian. It took time for everything to be translated into English. When we spoke, we had an interpreter with us, and I told him, This is where I'm going to include the schematic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. It's impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, the interpreters cannot follow you because you're speaking too quickly. Could you please try to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- slow down, and perhaps you resume your answer just a couple of lines ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very simple. Mr. Kay and I were talking. We went through a certain chapter in my expert report, and then I told Mr. Kay, This is where I want to add the schematic of the organisation of the Police Administration of Knin. I had it hand-drawn, based on the regulation on the internal organisation and the professional work of the Ministry of Defence. This is a decree that was adopted by the Government of the Republic of Croatia in February 1995. Mr. Kay looked at the part that I read out to him, and then he looked at my proposed schematic and told me, We already have that. This has already been admitted into evidence in the courtroom. There is no need for you to go into the trouble of producing the schematic. It is already there. We have it in an electronic form. And it, indeed, would have been very difficult for me to produce all the schematics in electronic form. It was as simple as that, and it applied to all the schematics. And when it comes to the central schematic of the MUP, since they had all the necessary support, I asked them to transform my proposal into an electronic form, which was easier for them to do than it would have been to me. And I apologise, Your Honours, for speeding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to take this meeting between you and Mr. Kay piece by piece. First of all, this meeting at which you and Mr. Kay are going through your report, and at which you're indicating to him you want to insert schematics, when exactly did this conversation take place, and where?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such conversations sometime in February or March. I really don't know exactly. I started working on my report in early February and finished. It's as simple as that. I can actually give you a practical demonstration of how things developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated February or March. Is that February or March of this year?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this year, 2009. It was after I stopped being a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you showed your schematics to Mr. Kay, and he looked at them and indicated that they'd already been admitted into evidence, at that time did he have -- the schematics which were admitted into evidence, did he have those with him to show you that they were identical?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a while, those schematics were downloaded from the database. As soon as he heard me describe my schematics, he was almost certain that we were talking about the same thing, because in the part that I gave to Mr. Kay there was a text and then there was the schematics of the Police Administration of Knin, and that schematic was hand-drawn by me. And when I spoke to Mr. Kay, Mr. Kay told me, The schematics already exist, they have already been tendered into evidence, and that's why we concluded that I should not have to go into the trouble of producing my schematics in the electronic form, since they already existed and had already been admitted into evidence. So we decided to adopt those. And Mr. Kay actually wanted to be absolutely sure and double-check whether the schematics that are already in evidence contain any mistakes, so we looked at them, and I was convinced that there were no mistakes, that they look exactly as they should, and that I could easily subscribe to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, how many such meetings did you have with Mr. Kay, where you went through the substance of your report and discussed what should or shouldn't be in there?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four, five at the most; not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And at each of these meetings, did you have a draft of your report with you to show Mr. Kay, or had you provided him with a draft of your report at that time prior to each of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I handed my report, and subsequently we had our meetings. How could we have had meetings without Mr. Kay being privy to the materials that I had produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When was the first time you handed your report to Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in February. I'm not very good with dates. First we discussed the contents. Then I told him what documents I was using to prepare my expert report. Then I drafted a certain number of chapters. And that's how our cooperation proceeded until the whole report was finalised. I don't have my notes on me, so I can't consult anything to be able to tell you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What I'm trying to determine, Mr. Kovacevic, is the extent to which you had meetings with Mr. Kay during the entire process of the drafting. In other words, you didn't, did you, hand a final report to Mr. Kay, and then have four or five meetings with him, and your report is exactly the same as the first time you handed it to him? That's not the case; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no major difference between my draft report and my final report. Mr. Kay wanted me to reduce the number of pages to bring it down to anything between 80 to 200 [as interpreted], not more. That's why I shortened some chapters concerning the presidential system in Croatia, the legal hierarchy of legal regulations, the jurisdiction over their passing, the role of some officials of the UN. Those things have not made it to the final version of my report. The only thing that happened was that the number of pages has been reduced in my final report. The essence of the report has not changed, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: How many drafts, exactly, did you give to Mr. Kay before achieving the final result?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, the second, and the third. The first was very extensive, and then Mr. Kay asked me to reduce the report to something between 80 and 100 pages, which would suffice. The second was a curtailed version, and then the third and final version was translated into English. And the two of us, together, checked and double-checked the translation, collated the translation with the original, in order to be as certain about the use of professional and technical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Misetic asked for two or three minutes in the absence of the witness. Could you find, within the next two or three minutes, a suitable moment to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not done with this topic, so this is just as good a time as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say you need any -- way more than two or three minutes. Then, Mr. Kovacevic, we'll have a break. We have first to deal with a procedural matter. I'm not yet aware of what it is, but we're not going to bother you with that. We'd like to see you back in close to half an hour from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, a matter we can deal with in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe and I just wanted to address the Chamber on this issue that was raised in cross-examination about documents being purchased on a black market. I understand Mr. Russo wasn't making an allegation and was exploring what was stated in the article, but we did want to be expressly clear that, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, we have never purchased any documents from anyone, and no documents tendered in this Chamber by the Gotovina Defence have ever been purchased or obtained on a black market or any such thing, just as officers of the Court, so that that is on the record. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Russo at least did not further pursue the matter once the witness had said how he obtained documents from the Defence. You add to this that whatever documents you obtained were not bought at the black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but I actually wanted it to be stated as fact on the record, that no such thing has taken place with the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, it's on the record, so that -- Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing bought on your black market, either, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nothing bought on the black market, and just for the record, the same thing applies to the Markac Defence as well as my learned friend told before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the same for me. And I didn't even buy Mr. Mikulicic a cup of coffee yesterday to get The Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just for me, since you make it an issue, I do understand that your statement says, We never paid for any document which we obtained from sources not in the government. That's what I understand by "black market," because I don't understand the government to be part of a black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I also wish to be clear about this, so there's no confusion. We've never paid the government for any documents, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was no suggestion of that kind in my observation, which does not mean that all the documents you ever obtained always were obtained from the government. I take it that whenever an individual was in possession of a document you considered to be useful, that you would obtain it from that individual, but you would not pay for it, and never you, I take it, you encountered a situation in which you were invited to pay for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Mr. President. The situation would be, again, Mr. Lausic's diary, it's a relevant piece of evidence in the private possession of the person. We would obtain a copy, and it's for our own use. Other examples would be media reports, et cetera, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I just want -- if you make a statement about the black market, where Mr. Russo asked about the black market and where the witness was not able to tell us anything about it, to have a proper understanding of what your clear statement, the statement of the Gotovina Defence, comes down to. And I take it, Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Kay, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it should be -- your statement should be understood in the same way. Then we'll have a break, and we'll resume at -- Mr. Russo, you paid for something?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm about to pay for a cup of coffee, Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All three Defence teams, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I can't promise that. I do intend to -- well, I had originally intended to put the chart to the witness. However, the testimony he's just given, I'd just like to ask him whether he knows the relationship between the ones in his report and Mr. Feldi's report, and I would like to bar table the comparison charts. I just thought I would give everyone a little notice of that. That's how I intend to proceed. So if there are any problems, I guess we can address them when we come back from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be of any use to, if we are comparing documents anyhow in view of the testimony of the witness, to compare what has been earlier tendered and was admitted into evidence with the dates, because now we have quite a lot of diagrams for which we have, well, various explanations as to how they were produced, by whom in handwriting, what was then done with it, for what purposes. And then now we have, as additional element, that simply documents that were already admitted into evidence were provided to the witness because they were apparently of the same contents as what the witness had produced, so that we have a full overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and we can certainly put something like that together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and can I make a statement, because it looks to me as though I'm prime suspect in all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not a suspect, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have used organigrams in the course of our cross-examination, as the Court knows, and in preparing this Defence case and having to learn a totally alien political and governmental structure, I have had organigrams produced for me so that I can see the picture and understand it, and it's a route that I have taken when introducing evidence at various points to help Your Honours in explaining it to you, the basis and nature of the structures that we are concerned with, as it occurred to me that during the presentation of this case that was lacking. And in my submission, it was done with all good intention to assist the parties. In the interim, a number of organigrams were obviously developed because the people I work with know this system, they're of it. Here's the man giving evidence who drafted the legal legislation. We've previously had General Feldi, who drafted the service regulations. They are people from the system, and any organigram that was produced would have been something that they would have seen and, if it was wrong or defective, would have not been in their report. I took the view that it was helpful as well, in their reports, to have organigrams in the text rather than as an annex, because it was easier to read and see, so it was an idea I had, in the preparation of the defence, to make sure that pictorially there was a representation for the Court and for others to see what was being said, rather than some exhibit footnote annex which you can't immediately relate to the text. So just to let Your Honours know that if an explanation is required, I am the person who thought organigrams would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I think there's no issue about organigrams or diagrams being useful. I think there were no objections to have them admitted into evidence. We have seen quite some of them. I think the issue that arose now is a bit of a different one; that is: Who is the intellectual author of the diagrams and organigrams we find in the expert reports? And that's -- we have now heard from this witness that he drafted his own ones, but then was provided with already existing ones already in evidence, whereas Mr. Feldi testified differently. He didn't say, Mine were, at the suggestion of the team, replaced by those already in existence; but he said, Mine were scanned, and then in its scanned version, they were introduced in my expert report. And then, of course, looking at the different -- the testimony about who authored what, exactly, then it may be interesting to compare the versions that were already in evidence, the versions that appear in one report, the versions that appear in another report, and versions that appear, as we know by now, in The Blue Book. And I think that's the matter we are exploring at this moment. And I did not gain any impression that the use of diagrams and preparing them would not be useful either for the case or for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, on another matter as well with General Feldi, I am -- have always been conscious in cases like these that the Prosecution use expert witnesses, I could not possibly deal with the expert report of Mr. Theunens on my own. I have had General Feldi as someone -- an expert to whom I could consult, and that was his purpose in coming and joining and working with my team. And I could not understand this system from the materials supplied in either the Prosecution pre-trial brief, indictment, or, indeed, the witness statements, and General Feldi has been a source of instruction to me. Any credit from my cross-examination, in a sense, is from those who I have to consult to understand these issues. And I just want to make that entirely clear and that there's nothing here that, in my eyes, is unusual in any litigation that I have ever conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kay, I don't think -- the issue there may be that if an expert appears before this Court who is employed by the Prosecution, that's usually known to the other parties and to the Bench. It appears in their CV that they were employed, when they were employed, which allows for questions such as, What subject matter did you deal with when you were employed? Whereas for Mr. Feldi, and I don't know to what extent it will be an issue to be raised by the Prosecution, but at least from his CV, it was not clear that he worked for the Cermak Defence team in the role as you just described, in addition to having been asked to prepare an expert report. That's, I think, what may have caused some questions to be put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I used him as an expert. Then I asked him to produce an expert report after Mr. Theunens had given evidence, and that is the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Russo, anything to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Nothing to be raised. I just wanted to advise the Trial Chamber that I'm aware I've only estimated two sessions. However, the pace of the cross-examination is not proceeding as I had hoped, and I think I may go more than two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to be as efficient as possible in this respect. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 7415, and my apologies. If I could also have the assistance of the Court Usher, I do have something to pass to the witness. This is the hard copy of the comparison chart of organigrams, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I want to take a look at just a few of the organigrams in your report and compare them to those in Mr. Feldi's report. If we could start with the first one, that is -- if we could move to the second page here in e-court. Actually, I believe it would be the third page. Yeah, the third page, please. And this is an organigram found at page 73 of your expert report. That's the B/C/S version. And if you take a look in your hard copy there, the document which appears next, if we could move to the next page in e-court, is the organigram which appears at page 20 of Mr. Feldi's report. And I've compared these two, and they appear to be identical. Now, I'd like you to explain to me, is this one of the organigrams which you had handwritten on your own and were told was already in the possession of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. There could be no differences between my diagram and Mr. Feldi's, because we used the same source. The source is the structure of the military police as prescribed by the minister of defence. The diagrams cannot differ if they are based on the same source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, did you get a look at Mr. Feldi's report before completing your own report?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not look at his report whatsoever, not before, not now, nor ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to be clear, you don't know, do you, exactly what the genesis of the organigrams that Mr. Feldi's included in his report were? You don't know where Mr. Feldi got those particular organigrams, do you?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Perhaps Mr. Kay could tell you, or someone else. Once I had made the handwritten diagram, Mr. Kay said he had it. I used the source, which was the Ministry of Defence. Therefore, there could have been no differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer 65 ter 7415 across the Bar table, and I will supplement with a submission regarding the use of similar organigrams in previous testimony, as the Court suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2638.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving on, I'd like to talk about some of the substance of your report, Mr. Kovacevic. If we could move to section 5.4.6 of your report. And for the benefit of the Court and counsel, this appears at page 97 in the English version and B/C/S page 89. In section 5.4.6, Mr. Kovacevic, you address the issue of military police subordination to HV commanders under Article 9 of the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police. And there you refer to several specific orders issued by General Lausic in August of 1995, orders in which he expressly subordinates military police to the highest HV commander in the area. And in particular, you state: "Finally, in neither of these two orders, orders dated 5 and 14 August 1995, did he explicitly and by himself specify the subordination of the Knin Military Police Company, since if that were the case, he would have used the expression 'I hereby subordinate,' instead of the word 'subordinate.'"

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There is a marked difference, "I hereby subordinate" and "to subordinate."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Kovacevic. Just waiting for the translation to catch up. Now, Mr. Kovacevic, are you attempting, in this section, to suggest to the Trial Chamber that there is some significance in the semantic distinction you're drawing here?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a significant difference. When one says "I hereby subordinate," it should be stipulated to whom. When it is stated "to subordinate," then we leave it up to someone else to do it. This is in the military jargon as well as in regular language. "I hereby subordinate" is something which takes effect immediately, and "to subordinate" denotes a lasting action. "To subordinate" is not as precise. It basically states that it is left to another person to do so. When I say "I hereby subordinate you to ...," that takes effect immediately. But when I say "to subordinate," that action has not taken place yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to be clear. Is it your opinion that if General Lausic had used the phrase "I hereby subordinate," then that would have been a legally-effective subordination of the military police to the HV? Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have read paragraph 5.4.5, you would have noticed several mistakes in his order. First of all, he used the term "in daily operational command." We don't find that term in Article 9 of the rules. It is simply not there. Secondly, the newly-formed platoons and companies which are to be subordinated to the most senior commander, he doesn't say to which commander and that they have been subordinated. Had he said, specifically, "Subordinate this and that company to the Knin commander," that would have been clearly -- clear and sufficient. Orders need to be clear, self-sufficient, and must be able to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, before deciding on what expression General Lausic would have used, did you actually review the evidence, that is, the witness statements and the testimony of General Lausic, regarding subordination of the military police to HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read his statements. As far as you can see, yourself, in this part I analyse it in legal terms. I analyse each component of his order, and I pointed out the mistakes he had made. That was my role, as the expert. I listened to that part of his testimony, and it is clear that he doesn't make a distinction between the various bylaws. Specifically, in this case, the organisational order for garrisons, in terms of the bylaws by the Ministry of Defence, which has to do with the basic mobilisation plan, one cannot use the Rules of Service for the Military Police to make a different decision. This is the legal hierarchy of the various regulations, and I realised from his testimony that he is not aware of that distinction. He tried to defend a position which, legally speaking, could not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you do not address Mr. Lausic's witness statements, nor any of the testimony he provided in court, in your expert report, and I'm going to suggest to you that you didn't do so because the evidence he provided, in fact, contradicts your theory about the applicability of Article 9. And I want to point you to some particular pieces of evidence that General Lausic provided. Specifically, at transcript page 15346, this is lines 15 to 17, General Lausic stated: "Article 9," and that's Article 9 of the rules, "envisaged the right to implement daily operational tasks in everyday activities to the various commanders of the armed forces in Croatia." If you'll bear with me, I'm going to read you a couple of other portions. At transcript page 15 --

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said is not foreseen by Article 9. If you actually read Article 9, you'll see that the terminology is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's helpful, if the witness can answer a proposition. We saw yesterday a wrapped-up ten or more quotes from the Prosecution which, in my submission, was unhelpful, and if the expert witness can respond as he wants to, to the proposition being put, I don't think that that's an unreasonable request on his behalf, nor unhelpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness did, as a matter of fact, and I did not have the impression that Mr. Russo was about to stop him on this matter. Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Russo will put several --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that does not appear on the transcript, at least. Mr. Russo, if -- there is a dilemma here, which is the following: Sometimes it is useful to respond to every single quote. Sometimes it is to be preferred to have them taken together. Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I would suggest the following: If you think that in that specific quote there is something that needs to be specifically addressed, and from what I understand, you have reviewed the testimony, and which is unrelated to other portions, then you can immediately respond. If, however, it is a matter which relates to other portions of the evidence which you have reviewed already, then I would suggest you wait until you have heard all of it and then respond to the quotes in their entirety. Mr. Russo, this dilemma might not be easily resolved, and be relied, to some extent, on the expert here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All of the pieces of evidence that I'm going to be referring to all deal with the exact same issue, so I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same issue, but not necessarily, I take it, all exactly the same testimony. To the extent you think you can deal with it altogether, Mr. Kovacevic, you're invited to wait until you've heard all of it. If you want to, at a later stage, want to be reminded of a specific portion, you can ask for that, say -- if you would say, I'd like to respond to the third quote you gave me, then we'll read that again to you, and then it may refresh your memory before you respond. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, at transcript page 15353, this is lines 19 to 25, General Lausic testified: "HV unit commanders or garrison commanders within whose area of responsibility the specific MP unit is, command MP units to execute all military policing tasks in keeping the authority and powers of work of the military police. They're also tasked with daily monitoring of the work of the MP and notify the MP Administration with the proposal of measures to be undertaken by the Administration so as to ensure efficient functioning of the MP unit." Now, before I move on to the other portions that I'm going to discuss, I'll give you an opportunity to respond to the first two quotes I've given.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One needs to say this: It is important that in all these situations, one needs to bear in mind the provisions of Article 9 and 10 of the Rules on the Structure and Work of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia. Article 10 is essential, because it sets out tasks. Article 10 is a combination of a corresponding article from the Law on Internal Affairs. These are the tasks of the basic police, crime police, and special police. So when Lausic speaks in such general terms, it is not correct. One needs to specify which tasks are to be assigned to the commanders of the military districts if any authority is given to them to command the military police. But the military police, as such, is outside the armed forces structure. It is under the Ministry of Defence, and he was the sole commander of the military police. The problem arises from what he is saying, which does not correspond to the legal reality. He cannot assign MP tasks to anyone else, and this includes the crime military police. He has to be very specific in terms of what regular, daily policing tasks are assigned to this and that particular military unit, say the battalion, and which tasks are assigned to the military district commander precisely. This is a legal regulation, and an order needs to be based on that. It has to be short, implementable, and clear. Otherwise, one might conclude that he had nothing to do with the military police and that it handed -- he handed over all of his authority to the military district commanders. Legally speaking, it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'll suggest to you, Mr. Kovacevic, that with respect to what tasks he is referring to as the HV commanders being able to direct the military police units with respect to, he indicates, as in the quote I read, all military policing tasks in keeping the authority and powers of the work of the military police. So to the extent that you indicate that he didn't specify, I suggest to you that, in fact, he did specify, and he specified all. But beyond that, I'd like you to point specifically -- if you can refer the Court to the language in either the rules or anything which actually says that the chief of the military police is required to specify X, Y, and Z in implementing orders. Can you point to a provision which says that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. Articles in question are on number 8, where it says that the chief of the administration commands the military police. Number 9 says that in the policing duties, HV units are subordinated to the head of the military district, which means that the legal provisions do not result in direct legal effects. What is necessary is a concrete military order which would specify the task. It says in Article 10 that there are three types of tasks: tasks of the basic police -- let's make, if you will allow me, let's make a distinction here. The military police does the same thing as the military police do -- as the civilian police do, but the military police is in charge of the armed forces. In any case, the tasks are the same. The tasks are the same, and there are also different tasks. And then an order should be issued where it will say, I hereby subordinate the military police to the military district commander, in terms of regular policing duties with regard to the military traffic, patrols, but it has to specify exactly what. This is the essence of the law, the essence of the order. And I wasted three months with them until I was able to draft the regulation to read properly. There is no "the most senior" that Lausic refers to. That term does not exist in the Croatian legislation, that term does not exist. He made it up. It's an invented term, invented by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just an observation. Could the witness be reminded by Your Honour, rather than me, to speak more slowly.
