utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried already, with my hands, to ask him. Mr. Kovacevic, in return, I got your gestures. If I use my hands, that is to remind you that you should slow down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, the Trial Chamber has heard quite a lot of evidence regarding applicability of Articles 8, 9, and 10. But to shortcut this section, would you simply agree with me that there is no particular language in the rules which states that Article 9 does not have a legal effect unless an implementing order is given? Would you agree with me that there is no language to be found which says that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we have to talk about legal rules and provisions, what provisions means and when they can have direct effects and when not. I'm saying that in Article 9, the provisions are drafted in such a way that they don't result in direct legal effects. They call for the passing of very specific orders. In other words, the provisions of Article 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're repeating your earlier testimony, explaining Article 9. The only thing Mr. Russo, at this point in time, asked you is whether you would agree that there is no particular language in the rules which states that Article 9 does not have a legal effect unless an implementing order is given. Now, whatever conclusions would that lead to, but if you say there is such language, clear language, please tell us. If not, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, you're not right, Your Honours. I am talking about legal positions and legal practice in the Croatian legislation system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asked whether you can point at any legal text, not how you interpret texts, because we have heard about that quite a bit, and it's clear what your position is. But Mr. Russo asked whether there is a specific rule which requires that Article 9 does not have a legal effect unless an implementing order is given, a specific implementing order. Now, if you can point to such a text, please do so. If not, it's fully clear what your position is, and then we can move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Russo is asking me is part of the Anglo-Saxon law, which doesn't exist in the Croatian legislation. There is no article of the same kind. And there is an important difference between the Continental Law and the Anglo-Saxon Law. The Continental Law stems from the Austro-Hungarian Law in Anglo-Saxon Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer, therefore, is that there is no such language to be found in the rules. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I notice, Mr. Kovacevic, that you don't treat Article 8 in the same fashion. Your opinion is that Article 8 is self-executing, as opposed to Article 9, which you claim is not self-executing. I wonder why you draw a distinction between those two situations.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Article 8 says that all units of the military police are subordinated to the Administration of the Military Police under the command of the chief of the military police; isn't that so? It's as clear as can be. General Lausic was the commander of the military police. And in Article 9, it says that in performing regular policing duties, units are subordinated to the commander of the military district. There is a major distinction there. One should specify tasks provided for in Article 10, what are the regular policing duties for which units are subordinated. I think it can't be any clearer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to refer back to some of the evidence of General Lausic. In his witness statement, that is P2159, paragraphs 194 to 195, General Lausic indicates that the 72nd Military -- 72nd Battalion Military Police Company based in Knin was subordinated to the highest military commander in its area of responsibility, which he defined as the town of Knin and its surrounding areas, and he stated that the highest-ranking Croatian Army commander in Knin at the time was General Cermak. Further on in that statement, at paragraph 249 General Lausic indicated that the Knin MP Company was under Cermak's command for its day-to-day activities and that if a crime was committed within Cermak's area of responsibility, it would have been his responsibility to direct the military police. Now, on cross-examination - this appears at transcript page 15662, lines 16 to 23 - Mr. Kay suggested to General Lausic that there was no document which established that the Knin MP Company was under the day-to-day command of General Cermak, but General Lausic disagreed with him and referred to Exhibit D47, which subordinates the MP company commander to the highest HV commander in the area. Now, what I'd like to know is -- or what I'm going to suggest to you is that you did not address this evidence in particular because it, in fact, contradicts your theory that this could not have been the case under Article 9. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have carefully read what I wrote in paragraph 549 and further on, I didn't find it anywhere in the case, in all the documents that I've perused, an order which would subordinate the company of the military police in Knin to anybody. There are just two Lausic's orders which say that somebody will have to do it, but he didn't specify who. If that was the nature of the order, if it was not conclusive, it should have been the battalion commander who had to do that, but he was never authorised. He had to authorise him by his order. In formal and legal terms... he could not, to General Cermak, as the commander of the garrison, because according to paragraph 2 of the order on organisation, the commander, or rather the command of the garrison does not have an operational function and the right to command over the armed forces. If he were to do so, he would violate the regulation issued by the Ministry -- or, rather, the Ministry of Defence about the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a mistranslation we're quite familiar with now. It was military garrison, not military district at 51, 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He could not "subordinate" instead of "order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That part of the translation will be verified, and I don't think that there's any unclarity as to the -- what the substance of the answer of the witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I just had to correct it in case anyone was misled by the transcript. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, are you familiar with an analysis put together by members and former members of the Main Staff regarding Operation Storm, an analysis which is commonly referred to as The Blue Book?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I never saw the book, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I heard about it from my colleagues in the Main Staff. I was with the Ministry of Defence until the year 2000. I heard that they were putting together a book about Operation Storm. I don't know when that materialised, whether it was in 2005, or 2006, or 2007, but I knew that the publishing section of the Main Staff was doing something to that effect. I never saw the book. I only heard that its name -- its title was either "The White Book" or "The Blue Book." I really don't know what the title is, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you provide us with the names of the individuals who you heard were working on this book?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never told any names, and it's very difficult for me to remember anything. I didn't see the book; I didn't read the book; I didn't know whether it's blue or red, so I can't really be of much use to you in that respect, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7416. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this is a -- these are several pages which are excerpts from the CD version of The Blue Book which we received yesterday. And if we could focus on the -- just on the footnote at the bottom of this page and enlarge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, would you please do me a favour and read that footnote into the record.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Complete command as a military responsibility of a superior officer to issue orders to his subordinates. It covers all the aspects of military operations and administration." It's a very strange footnote. There should be a definition of "complete command" as opposed to "incomplete command."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page, please, and focus on the very first footnote on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, could you read into the record the portion which defines "Operativno zapovijedanje"?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you using me as a speaker here now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, if you read slowly. The problem is that this document has not yet been translated, and you are right that we are using, or one could even say, abusing you as a native-speaking person. But if you would adopt approximately the speed of speech as I now demonstrate, then the interpreters and transcribers will be able to follow you. So could you please slowly read which, Mr. Russo, seems to be still a part of footnote 517 which starts at the previous page. Yes, could you please slowly read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so: "Operational command as an authority vested in a commander, allowing him to assign missions or tasks to subordinated commanders, to deploy units, or re-subordinate forces, and to maintain or delegate operational and/or tactical control as needed. This does not include responsibility for administration or logistic. It can also be used to mark the forces assigned to the commander." Shall I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, thank you. One last portion to read, if we could go to the next page. I promise this is the last abuse I will make of you in this regard, Mr. Kovacevic. But if we could focus on footnote 537. It's the very last footnote on the page. And if you could read the entire footnote slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pursuant to the provisions of the rules on the organisation work of the military police of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia stipulated in Article 8, all," and this is a quote, "'All military police units are subordinated to the Administration of the Military Police of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia under the administration and the command of the chief of the Administration of the Military Police.' Daily operational command is defined by Article 9 of the same regulation," and I quote, "'In performing regular military policing duties, military police units are subordinated to the commander of the military district, the commander of the Croatian Navy, the commander of the Croatian Air Force, or to the highest-ranking commander of the Croatian Army in the territory where the military police are active. Thus, the Administration of the Military Police of the Ministry of Defence had full command authority over the units of the military police, whereas the commanders of the military districts had the authority of operational command for -- over the military police units assigned to them in the performance of daily tasks and duties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it is important. The word "po duznosti," the third line from bottom, was read out but not translated. That means "by function," so I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking the -- well, let's first -- I don't remember what was exactly read. I did not follow it. Any disagreement, Mr. Russo, that a word may have been missing and that we should -- perhaps we could ask the witness to read that word again. Is it possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 54, line 23 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just ask the witness to read the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That portion again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- apparently, Mr. Kovacevic, there was one word missing in what you read, or it was not heard by the -- could you please -- I think it's the last sentence, Mr. Kay, if -- yes. Could you please read again, slowly, the last sentence of footnote 537.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Frustrating. The third-to-last line of the extract, if that line, which starts beginning with "Navisem po duznosti ..." I won't try anymore to murder a language that I struggle with, but if that could be read out and the translation given. I think it can be taken from us that we would only be objecting on this for good cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, but at the same time we have a procedure to have on the record not what, although for good reasons has been suggested by counsel, but what was read and what was translated, interpreted for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Could you -- could you start reading at the line Mr. Kay suggested, and read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The most senior commander of the HV by function in the territory where the MP unit is active."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, does this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and it's been a live issue in the case, as Your Honour knows. That's why I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, do you agree with what's been stated in footnote 537 that you've read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to note one objection, and that is that the actual sentence from the main text, which is where the footnote then comes, which is if we go into the main text on page 1, it says this terminology is taken from NATO publications and that the authors are using this terminology simply for the benefit of the reader. This terminology, at least from this text, is not terminology used in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is comment rather than anything else. You could have sought to clarify this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, because it's misleading, both first to the Court, since we don't have an English translation as to what this terminology is about, and do you agree with what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the text as written here. A text was read, and now Mr. Russo asks whether the witness agrees with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether that is NATO or whether it is Australian or whether it's Colombian, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question is, does he agree that that is what the term means where? Recall that we started -- he started having him read on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- we'll ask whether the witness agrees with what's written, and we could ask him what his understanding is of what is presented in this text. Mr. Russo, at the same time you've heard the objection raised by Mr. Misetic. If you would rephrase your question in light of that, and then, of course, you're invited to do so. This, of course, is to some extent a result of not having a translation of this text yet available. We have to deal with the shortcomings of the situation. At the same time, it could not lead to everyone explaining why this portion is read. We can ask the witness what he understands this to be and whether he agrees with it. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, irrespective of whose interpretation this may be or in what context it may apply, the language that you read in footnote 537, do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, of course I agree with the quotes taken from Articles 8 and 9. However, I would like to add something to the last sentence or, rather, to the last part of that sentence which reads: "Over the MP units assigned to them in the performance of their daily tasks," it should read, "in the performance of regular policing duties, as stipulated in Article 9." I wouldn't know what "daily tasks" would be, because they have not been specified. The regulation is more precise in that respect. What I'm saying is that they are shortening, summarising, and making a mistake, because they are transforming regular policing tasks and duties into daily tasks and duties, which compounds the matter even further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Russo, could we invite the witness to read the main text preceding footnote 537 and to complete reading that sentence, and ask him whether having read this would cause him to in any way supplement or change his answer. Therefore, we have to move on a little bit higher to see where the sentence starts and then to give an opportunity to the witness. Apparently, it starts with "Postrojbe." And could an opportunity be given to the witness as well to read the remaining part of this sentence on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The problem is, Mr. President, there is no next page. I don't know what it says. I'm happy to get it from the CD and have it brought in, but that was not part of the excerpt which I brought in. So there is no next page to turn to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, I've listened to Mr. Misetic's objection, and I want to -- on the one hand, to avoid that we are telling the witness what is relevant in understanding the text. At the same time, I would like that, if there is some concern, to give a fair opportunity to look at the main text in order to better understand the context in which the footnote was created. Now, Mr. Mikulicic, you are offering us the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I am offering an assistance, if Your Honour pleases. The relevant main text is under the footnote 517, which is on first page of this extract that Mr. Russo provide us, so maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that during the next break you will assist Mr. Russo in finding the context in which you consider relevant and which would shed perhaps a different light on texts and footnotes and try to agree with him on the basis of the text, that it -- what would be fair to put to the witness. We are struggling with the absence of a translation. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll do that, if the Chamber desires. However, I do want to note that I have a general objection to the use of this document at all, because I don't -- I was going to wait until Mr. Russo tried to tender it, but I don't think this document is admissible into evidence to begin with. And if you wish to hear it now, I'd be happy to state my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you briefly, because an objection to an admission into evidence of a document which has not yet been tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, just to see if we need to do all this work during the break, et cetera, on a document that may not ultimately be admitted. I think the parties are in agreement and the Prosecution cross-examined General Feldi yesterday on the principle that The Blue Book was prepared at the request of the Markac Defence for purposes of this proceeding. As such, this Blue Book falls either under Rule 92 bis or 92 ter, if it's not an expert report. If it's an expert report, it falls under Rule 94 bis. But either way, it's prepared for purposes of this proceeding. It's just like a witness statement taken by the Prosecution and disclosed to the Defence, which the Defence tried to tender Prosecution statements in its case in-chief and the Chamber denied it. So I would argue that this report is -- was prepared, at least from the evidence we have, for no other reason than these proceedings, and as such, unless there's some way for the Prosecution to fulfill the requirements of Rules 92 or 94 bis, it's inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that once the document has been tendered. At this moment, we're just reading a quote from a document which, apart from providing information, also played a role in the activities of Expert Witness Feldi when preparing his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would draw the distinction there, Mr. President, which is why I didn't object yesterday, to -- if it goes to issues of credibility, then the matter is not being submitted for the truth or the substance of the matters in the report. My impression is that Mr. Russo intends to tender this for the substance of the report now, which changes the calculus, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he invites the witness to give his views on what is written somewhere. Let's proceed at this moment, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I want to try to cut things a little short. And I just want to make it clear to you, if it's not clear already, what the Prosecution's position is with respect to military police subordination. It is the Prosecution's position that the military police were under the command of General Cermak in the area of Knin and also under General Gotovina in the Split Military District. Now, first of all, are you aware that that's the Prosecution's position?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just said so, but it is incorrect regarding General Cermak and General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, to start with, was whether you are aware that it is the position of the Prosecution. You are not invited to tell us whether you agree or disagree, but whether you were aware that this is the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You put it to me. Now I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And specifically with respect to the evidence of Basko Dzolic, which I understand from your expert report you reviewed in conducting your analysis, I'll put to you that the evidence provided by Mr. Dzolic taken in, you know, its context, supports the Prosecution's position and also supports the testimony of General Lausic that the Knin MP Company was subordinated to General Cermak. Now, having reviewed all of the testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I finish my question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there's been a misrepresentation of the evidence in the case. I had to sit quietly yesterday while it happened, but I am very, very concerned about evidence being taken that misrepresents the evidence in the trial. I feel that if the Defence had done that during the Prosecution case, we would have been corrected, Your Honour. And so before Your Honour interjects, I want to show that this is an objection we have which is fundamental, because if you put something to a witness, saying, Someone else says this, and it's incorrect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's try and keep matters simple. I do understand that the witness reviewed this evidence. Why characterising it then? And then, Mr. Russo, why don't you ask, Having reviewed the evidence given by Mr. Dzolic and by Mr. -- who else was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lausic. Whether the witness could elaborate on why he disagrees with certain portions of it, rather than to say, This is in support of, or this demonstrates this or that? Just keep it in rather neutral terms. Then we avoid whatever problem of misrepresenting, whether it supports or does not support. Let's hear what the witness's comment is on this evidence, compared to his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, Mr. President, I think there is a problem with my not being permitted to put my position on the evidence to the witness. I believe it's part of my obligation to indicate to the witness what I believe the evidence to indicate, and if he disagrees with me, he can indicate to me why he disagrees with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, you're not required to put every piece of evidence, and if you want to put the evidence to the witness, there's -- Mr. Kay has no problem with that. The problem is that you are telling that this is in support, which means that you already give your appreciation of the evidence. Whether it supports or not, of course, I take it that you consider it supportive for the Prosecution's position, but that's irrelevant for the witness to know. I would say, important is to what extent this evidence, of which you may think whether it's supportive or not, what comments this witness, who apparently differs of opinion on certain matters, as expressed in that evidence, what his comment on it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I have to disagree, respectfully, with Your Honour. I do believe that under 90(H), which is a rule of fairness to the witness, I do believe I have to preface these questions by advising the witness that the evidence that I'm going to put to him -- advising him that, in my view, it supports my case. It's to allow the witness to address the evidence I'm going to suggest to him in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's listen to your question, and I do understand that you disagree, but you're nevertheless encouraged to put it to the witness in such a way that the type of objections raised by Mr. Kay will not result from your questions. And if you are falling short of any other -- of any obligation under Rule 90(H), I trust that Mr. Kay will raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to refer you to, Mr. Kovacevic, particular pieces of Mr. Dzolic's testimony, and again I'm going to do those seriatim and then ask you some questions about them. But you indicated that you have reviewed the testimony of Mr. Dzolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched his testimony when I was working on that part of my report dealing with General Cermak reporting on some arson. You can find it in my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. And before I move on to the specific pieces I want to address with you, I do want to make a it clear, in case you hadn't seen this portion of the evidence, at transcript pages 9017, lines 16 to 18, as well as transcript pages 9035 to 9037, this is upon questioning by Mr. Kay. Mr. Dzolic in fact indicated that he was not under the command of General Cermak and that General Cermak could not issue orders to him. I do want to make it clear that in case you hadn't read that testimony, he did testify to that on cross-examination. Now, what I'd like to put to you are some of the statements he made before he gave that evidence on cross-examination and ask you whether you considered those. Now, in his first statement to the Prosecution, Mr. Dzolic stated that he was asked -- and I'm sorry, for the benefit of everyone, this is at P875, paragraph 37 of the statement. In that paragraph, Mr. Dzolic stated that he was asked by his superior, Colonel Budimir, to be at General Cermak's disposal, and he understood that to mean that he was partly under General Cermak's command and partly under Colonel Butmir's command, and that he was to obey any order that General Cermak gave him. In a subsequent statement that Mr. Dzolic made to the OTP, he made a correction to that very same paragraph that I've just referenced, but he did not change that particular statement about receiving orders or responding to orders issued by General Cermak. Now, prior to confirming the accuracy of his statements, Mr. Dzolic was given an opportunity to review the statements that he made on the morning of his testimony, and he, in fact, made several corrections -- clarifications to those. However, he did not change anything in paragraph 37, which I've just referenced for you, or the paragraph, which is paragraph 15 of his second statement, which makes reference to paragraph 37 of the first statement. And then Dzolic testified that if he was asked the same questions as he was asked in those statements, if he was giving the same answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you're emphasizing at this moment how serious we should take this portion of the statement. We don't have to go through all the procedural details. I mean, if there's any need, the other parties will ask you, but this is really -- just put to the witness what is in his statement, and then you have already referred to the fact that, in cross-examination, the matter was revisited, and let's -- because what you're actually doing - I hope you're aware of that - you're emphasizing that there could be no doubt as to this is really what he meant to say. Let's just put the statement to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: During his testimony, Mr. Dzolic testified on direct examination -- this is at transcript page 8953, lines 20 to 21: "I was invited by General Cermak to come there for a conversation because I was subordinate to him in the daily tasks." Now, I take it from what I've read in your expert report that you endorse the retraction that Mr. Dzolic made on cross-examination, that he was not subject to the orders of General Cermak, rather than endorsing the statements he had made previously regarding his subordination to General Cermak. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Dzolic was not subordinated to General Cermak, and the military police in Knin was not subordinated to General Cermak. It could not have been, for the reasons I have explained in detail in my report in footnotes -- sorry, in paragraphs 541 to and including 549.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, I'd like your explanation for why you didn't choose to endorse the evidence which Mr. Dzolic gave prior to his cross-examination. Why, in your opinion, having looked at the evidence, why not give that credit over his retraction on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't do that at all. I simply wrote my expert opinion. I did a legal analysis rather than dealing with Dzolic's statements. I didn't use that as a basis for my expert report. It would be a dilettante thing to do. I used legal regulations to draft a professional expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you indicating that you didn't rely on any of the testimony given by any of the witnesses in this case, or any evidence other than legal regulations, before you formed your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The laws and regulations, yes. I did refer to Dzolic's statement or testimony, and I can tell you exactly in which part of my expert report it refers to the specific cases. It is in Chapter 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll try to cut this matter short. Mr. Russo, in the previous answer the witness said that he explained, in his report, why the initial statement of Mr. Dzolic is wrong. Now, you have referred to his statement and you have referred to retracting that position, saying that Mr. Dzolic was not subject to the orders, where earlier he said that he had to come for a conversation because he was a subordinate to him. Now, it appears to me, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that this witness prefers the second position taken by Mr. Dzolic on the basis of his analysis, right or wrong, of the legal structure and the legal texts. That seems obvious to me. Are you seeking for any other reasons or -- because that's what the witness said, Mr. Dzolic is wrong because I've written that in my report, what the real subordination system was, so he must have been wrong with his first answer. Whether this expert is right or wrong, and what the importance is of Mr. Dzolic thinking that he was subordinate or not thinking that he was a subordinate, is another matter. But what do you expect now the witness to say, other than what he has said in his analysis of the legal structure, legal texts?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, first of all, I have a problem with indicating to the Trial Chamber, in front of the witness, what the purpose is of the questions I'm asking, because I don't want to tip him off. But since the Trial Chamber wants to know, I'll indicate to you now, since I'm going to move on with this line of questioning. What I'm attempting to demonstrate is that Mr. Dzolic formed his opinions on the basis of whatever he says he formed his opinions about, and that he was unwilling to revisit the opinions he made or the conclusions he drew based upon the Prosecution's evidence, and that, in fact, he's already indicated by his testimony, at least that's what I'm attempting to get him to confirm, that I believe he used the words "only a dilettante would do that," would refer to the evidence which has been presented to change an opinion he's already drawn. I'm trying to establish that the witness came to a preconceived conclusion and did not make a neutral and objective analysis of all of the evidence presented before forming his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which raises the issue as the relevance and importance of the testimony of a witness in forming an opinion as an expert on legal structure. That's the issue. I'd suggest that you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could have just a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, to conclude, I can tell you that I did read the testimony in the case of arson of some houses in Knin. I have read that part of the statements, and it's all in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to raise this in the approach of my learned friend saying, I'm trying to establish that the witness came to a preconceived conclusion and did not make a neutral and objective analysis. When this whole questioning starts off with a description of the witness saying one thing, and then on cross-examination, and I'll refer Your Honours to it, at lines -- at page 9037, line 3, contradicting the proposition that's being put by my learned friend as the basis of his questioning. So to accuse the witness of coming to a preconceived conclusion when the materials he relies upon are fundamentally flawed, as the Court will see and as he's admitted in the preamble to the question, that -- I'm sorry, but I don't want my witness confused or misled, or this exercise to have some sort of impact on the proceedings, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you. We could go on with this for a long time. Apparently, the focus of Mr. Russo is somewhere, and it might not have been very wise of me to invite him to explain that, or perhaps he should have asked the witness to take off his earphones. That would have been a better solution. The focus should be on understanding what this expert tells us. Now, if he has considered evidence given at another moment before this Trial Chamber, then, of course, we could be very selective, emphasizing what he said first and then emphasizing what he said in cross-examination, still to be considered in the totality of the evidence, which part of the evidence should be given more weight or less weight. The Chamber will consider that in its entirety, but more or less to put the most favourable portions of the evidence and then say, Why didn't you follow that? Or put another portion and say, Why didn't you follow that? I think this expert has provided us with his interpretation of the rules, the applicable rules at the time, and what we see is that we had various statements, that we have various pieces of evidence either in favour of this interpretation or in that interpretation. Now, it's clear what the interpretation of this witness is. And of course there's nothing wrong with asking specific questions to the witness in relation to earlier evidence, but let's try not to draw all kind of conclusions as with what intention someone may have rightly interpreted or misinterpreted a legal context, and why he didn't pay more attention to this or more attention to that. Let's try to keep it clear, and let's take 20 minutes to think it over, how to achieve that. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, in relation to Articles 8, 9, and 10, Mr. Russo, but I'm also addressing Defence counsel, quite a lot of hairs have been split. New evidence may result in these hairs to be split again, but perhaps with different results. Now, for the Chamber, it is important to know how the hair looks once being split by A, B, C, and D. However, the Chamber is not interested that much in a comparative analysis of the tools used when splitting that hair, the light that was there when we looked at the result at a certain moment. We should just accept that the hair is split in different ways by different parties, by different experts, by different witnesses. We'll look at it in its entirety at the end, and the parties are not encouraged to see, unless, of course, there's good cause to do so, whether there is another hair to be found that could be split in the same context, or to again, as I said, compare the splitting exercise in every single detail. You may proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, now, am I right in interpreting your report as looking at the situation as it should be according to your interpretation of Croatian laws and regulations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly correct. This is only partly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain what other part is not correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my methodology, I specified and clarified how the expert report was drafted and what it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I've read the portion of your report where you indicate the methodology, but it's unclear to me whether you were offering an opinion about the way the situation actually unfolded on the ground or whether you were offering a position as to what was -- what should have happened on the ground, according to legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion encompasses both aspects. I'm talking about my expert report, and I'm saying that it encompasses both aspects of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So to be clear, you're offering an opinion about what, in fact, General Cermak's authority was in Knin at the time relevant to the indictment; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, yes. I don't understand what you are asking me. What is it that you want to hear from me? Can you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, you've answered my question, Mr. Kovacevic. Now, you've come to the conclusion that General Cermak was not authorised to issue orders to the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if I showed you orders that were issued by General Cermak to the military police, would that change the opinion that you've formed?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't change that, and I have to explain why, perhaps. There are some orders which --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... stop you there. At this point, I'm not interested in why you wouldn't accept -- or why you would not change your opinion. I just want to be clear. And it's also your opinion that General Cermak did not have authority to issue orders to the civilian police; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is correct. He was not part of the civilian police system. How could he issue orders to them? He did not have any legal right to do that. The Ministry of Defence [as interpreted] is a state ministry, and it was well known who could issue order to the police, and that's why we have the structure of the ministry and all police administrations. There is no state in the world where a military will be allowed to issue orders to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe there's an error in translation in line 21, when it's mentioned "the minister of defence." I suppose the witness mentioned some other ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you said, talking about issuing orders to the civilian police, you said, about Mr. Cermak, "he did not have any legal right to do that." Then you referred to a ministry and said this was a state ministry, and it was well known who could issue an order to the police. What ministry were you referring to at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of the Interior. That's the ministry I was referring to, and that was a state ministry, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, if I showed you orders issued by General Cermak to the civilian police, would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it won't change my opinion. In my expert report, I specified some situation from practice, showing that commanders issued orders to civilian bodies which they were not authorised to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, the point I'm attempting to make here, and let me see if you agree with me: Irrespective of your opinion as to whether or not those orders could legally be issued, did you consider the fact that -- the fact that they were issued, did you consider that that might indicate that the situation on the ground is not as it is reflected in your opinion of what it should have been?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I even found statements issued by some witnesses who stated that those orders were treated as information by those who received them, which is in keeping with my legal point of view and with the legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you -- well, if I showed you evidence which indicates that people who received orders from General Cermak treated them or at least referred to them as orders or commands, would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't change my opinion. My opinion is exact, it's based on regulations, it's based on statements, and every case can be looked on its own, in its entirety, and we can then clarify anything that may not be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, in the methodology section of your report, you indicate that you conducted an analysis of "all documents and evidence referring to the case in question." Can you tell me, in reviewing all of that evidence, did you find any evidence at all which indicates, on its face, that General Cermak did, in fact, have authority to issue orders to the military police or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find a single piece of evidence indicating that General Cermak was authorised to issue orders to the police, and I did find documents showing that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you find any evidence to suggest that the orders that he did issue were, in fact, followed by the people he ordered to follow them?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was something with regard to the restriction of movement, the initial restriction of movement, but that was all cancelled when the Police Administration of Split and Dalmacija warned General Cermak that he was not authorised to restrict the movement of people or issue any sort of passes to that effect. That was within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, or the Ministry of Defence, or military commanders at the level of military districts when combat activities are going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you point me to the piece of evidence that you reference here about a warning issued to General Cermak? Can you point me to that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on me. I saw the document. I don't have it on me. This document was issued by the Police Administration of Split and Dalmacija, the chief of the Police Administration wrote to the MUP. I was with the Ministry of Defence at the time. I got a call from the Chief of the Main Staff, and I said that he, as a commander, did not have the authority to restrict movement or issue passes to that effect, that this was within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, or the Ministry of Defence, or the commander of the military district pursuant to Article 150 something of the Law on Defence. And, finally, when things came to a head, it was decided that some actions were against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacevic, am I correct in interpreting your answer? Are you saying that you got a call from somebody in the -- the Chief of the Main Staff? Are you saying that you were involved in this warning to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cervenko was the chief of the Main Staff, and he asked me for a piece of legal advice when it came to that. He asked me about the restriction of movement, who was in charge of that, and then I provided my interpretation of the law and told him within whose purview was that. General Cervenko, while he was Chief of the Main Staff and chief of the military office, always consulted me about any military issues because I was the one who had drafted all the laws and regulations within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, can you tell us where we can find in your report any indication of the fact that you were issuing legal advice regarding the actions of General Cermak at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I did not put that anywhere in my report. You asked me a very specific question. You asked me about a concrete case, and then you followed up on that, and I then told you exactly how the whole situation unfolded with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When exactly did you get this call from General Cervenko regarding the actions of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to remember as I sit here today. It was sometime in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kovacevic, did you review the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, it all started with the warning. Are you able to identify, if at all, in what document we can find this warning? Is it footnoted in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already told you that this is not in my report. Mr. Russo asked me if I am aware of any such specific and concrete situation, so I referred him to a document issued by the chief of the Police Administration of Split and Dalmacija, who reacted and said that General Cermak was acting against the law. This is not in my expert report. I was answering Mr. Russo's question, and I illustrated my answer with that example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you say we do not find a reference to that document in your report. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, did you -- in conducting your analysis, did you consider the evidence provided by General Cermak in the interviews that he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did read that statement. But what do you want to know, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, in his 2004 interview with the Office of the Prosecutor - that's Exhibit P2532 - this appears at page 20 in the English, the B/C/S is also in the same transcript, General Cermak states that General Gotovina had the entire military police under him. Do you recall reading that part of General Cermak's interview?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that detail, but I believe that he misspoke, because it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Do you think -- is it your opinion that he's lying about that or simply uninformed?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, General Cermak did not have military knowledge and skills with regard to the legal issues and regulations. Maybe he believed that to be the case. In other words, he did not have a full legal picture which would enable him to answer all the questions correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kovacevic, wouldn't you agree with me that General Cermak would have a better picture than you about what the situation actually was in Knin and around the area in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly are you referring to when you use the term "picture"? What are you referring to? General Cermak did not have complete knowledge and information about all the regulations, laws, and orders that we are discussing today and which make part of my report. He did not have that knowledge and information. Otherwise, he would not have provided a statement of that kind, because full control of military police, when you say that, that means that the military police is not under the Administration of the Military Police and Lausic, which is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm not asking you to give me your opinion about whether he's correct or not correct. First of all, you don't know what General Cermak knows or doesn't know about the laws and regulations; right? I mean, you're assuming that he doesn't know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is fair --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know it either, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question posed to him, Is it your opinion General Cermak is lying, and then he provided an answer as to what his opinion was. I'm sorry, if I can look at the question again. It says then -- then he follows up after he gets the answer by saying, I'm not asking you to give me your opinion, which is exactly what he did ask for in the prior question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the prior questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I can respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question was about the better picture. This line of questioning, Mr. Russo -- I'll be careful. What happens, as a matter of fact, is the expert is -- when he talks about the full picture, he's primarily talking about the legal picture. If you are talking about the picture on the ground, you're apparently referring to something else. And then to ask, Wouldn't he have a better picture, it depends on what picture you have on your mind, because authority -- exercise of authority has both the legal aspects and can be viewed in very factual terms as well. You can ask yourself what was the legal authority of a person at a certain moment, and you can ask yourself whether that person behaves in line with what you would consider to be his legal authority or that he would, in his behaviour, show that either he had a different opinion on his authority or that, with full knowledge of the authority, he just didn't behave in accordance with it. That's, in short, the situation I think we are talking about. And let's try to clearly identify what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, at transcript page 78, line 6 to 8, I asked the witness whether General Cermak would have a better picture than you about what the situation actually was in Knin." I don't know any other way to explain or express to the witness the distinction I'm attempting to draw between what he says the situation should be and what the situation actually was. I think the witness understood my question. The answer he provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then he immediately went to his view on the matter. Going back to the legal authority, that's the reason why I tried to explain - and, Mr. Kovacevic, you'll certainly have understood this - what Mr. Russo, when he talks whether you have a clear picture on what happened on the ground, what he's asking is whether Mr. Cermak would know better than you or whether the behaviour that could be observed at that time was in line with what you consider to be consistent with authority in abstract legal terms. That's what Mr. Russo is trying to find out. Mr. Russo, unless I've misunderstood you. Could you -- so on the behaviour on the ground, could you tell us whether Mr. Cermak would have a clear view on that, at least, irrespective of whether he understood all the details of the legal aspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had a misperception. I don't know what he meant when he said that. What did he mean when he said to have under him, to have full control, what did he mean? I am saying that he had a misperception from the point of view of the legislation of the Republic of Croatia and of all the regulations. It's very difficult to answer a question about a picture because we have to go into that -- deeper into that to see what General Cermak actually meant. If I knew that, I would be able to provide you a proper, correct answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo is asking you not what he meant in saying that, but Mr. Russo is asking whether -- what your knowledge and to what extent you considered what actually happened on the ground, in terms of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have taken everything into consideration. I said that in the methodology part. There were situations where things were done against the law, and that was subsequently corrected. Commanders would issue orders that they were not authorised to do. When that was realised and established, there were sanctions, and such orders were withdrawn. Laws are laws. They have to be implemented. Regulations are regulations. One cannot and should not issue orders for which they are not authorised. This is the principle according to which a state with a rule of law functions. And if you learn of such instances, you have to react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One line in your answer said you cannot and you should not issue orders you're not authorised to give. Would you agree with me that you can, but that you should not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, just a very short answer. Did General Cermak or anyone on General Cermak's behalf tell you what General Cermak knew about the subordination of either the military police or the civilian police to him in August, September, October, and December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. You're talking about a problem that General Cermak had? He was in reserve. He was out of the action for a long number of years, and then he went down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Did you talk to General Cermak about what happened in this case?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did anyone on behalf of General Cermak tell you what General Cermak knew or believed about his authority in Knin and the surrounding area between August and the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From documents that I perused, I could see that he was not very clear about his authorities at first, but gradually he became much better versed and he became more knowledgeable in that respect, which is only understandable. He had been in reserve. Then he was appointed again. He did not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, my answer [sic] was: Did anyone, on behalf of General Cermak, tell you what General Cermak knew or believed about his authority in the area at the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "anyone"? I looked at documents, and I told you what was my basis for answering your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that you formed an opinion on the basis of documents. The question of Mr. Russo is whether ever anyone came to you, saying, Mr. Cermak considers this or this or that to be his authority, whether anyone told you what Mr. Cermak thought about what his authority was, not what you concluded from documents, but whether someone came and told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, okay. I believe that on one occasion, the late General Cervenko told me, It seems to me that General Cermak doesn't really know what his authorities actually are. It was during an informal conversation when we were talking about the passes that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions. I do have the printed-out pages of the material that I asked the witness to read earlier. I have the entire section here. If we -- if the Court wants to go through that exercise, I leave it to the Trial Chamber, but I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Use your microphone, and then we could hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: People are helping me, and I'm finding -- excuse me, Your Honour. I'm just trying to find something that was e-mailed to me. Ah, here it is. Sorry, Your Honour. Just something that arose towards the end of cross-examination by my learned friend, and I want to be exact with the text, and finding it takes a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you told us that in August 1995 you were working in a certain position and General Cervenko had occasion to speak to you. What was your position at that time in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the chief of the Department for Supervision of the Implementation of Regulations in the Ministry of Defence, the chief of the Department for the Supervision of the Implementation of Regulations of the Legal Administration of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And General Cervenko would speak to you about what kind of matters?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cervenko spoke to me daily, almost, on different legal issues pertaining to the implementation of the existing regulations on various issues. He frequently asked me to come to his office and sought my legal opinion on the various legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to the matter you raised concerning General Cermak at the time, a legal issue that General Cervenko spoke to you about, you made a comment about General Cervenko's view concerning General Cermak. Could you tell us, as much as possible, what he said about General Cermak's knowledge of his role?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Cervenko told me something to the extent that it seemed to him that General Cermak was not aware of his authority, as the garrison commander. He also said that it was understandable because he was not an active serviceman and many things had changed in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked various questions concerning the testimony of General Lausic concerning Article 9, and I want to read out to you a passage of his testimony, transcript page 15606 to 15607. It won't be -- it's not in your report, Mr. Kovacevic. It's -- General Lausic gave evidence earlier in the proceedings. You've been asked about various aspects of testimony, and I want to put to you something he said for your comment. He was asked this question in relation to a document dated the 14th of August, and it was this: "So just looking at that, in the terms of this order, your commander of the 72nd in Knin, Budimir, was required to do a positive act of subordinating the commander of the newly-established company of the Knin Military Police to the most senior Croatian military commander by function in the zone of responsibility, isn't that right, that required him to do a positive act to ensure subordination took place?" His answer was: "Correct. Based on this order that I issued, all battalion commanders from whose battalions, the newly-established platoons, and the company in Knin were formed had to specify how this item 14 was to be implemented." So this concerned subordination of any of the military police battalions and the mechanism, if that was to be take place, how it was to happen. What is your comment there on the answer of General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This answer is correct, and I have also discussed it in my expert report. It was necessary to issue an implementation order. This is what General Lausic said as well. In his view, this was supposed to have been done by the commander of the 72nd MP Battalion, and the other commanders that the order would include, legally speaking, Lausic said that they should have been determined, and he rightfully says that this was supposed to have been carried out by the commander of the 72nd Battalion, which he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Could you give me an indication as --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I hope to finish in less than five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than five minutes. I'm also looking at the other Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, let me just ask you a few questions on the basis of the famous Article 8 and 9 now. The 1994 rules, February of 1994, do you agree with me that those were rules passed within the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, these are the rules of the Ministry of Defence, i.e., bylaws put in force by the minister of defence based on the amendments and changes to the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As such, therefore, they are -- those rules are binding for persons who are subordinated to the minister of defence within the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to bring those rules for all those employed in the Ministry of Defence. It was based on Article 152 of the Law on Defence. This was a bylaw which is binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: In and of itself, would the rules require -- let me ask it a different way. General Lausic, as the chief of the Military Police Administration, could not issue orders to operational commanders or to HV commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lausic had nothing to do with the operative commands of the HV. General Lausic was commander of the military police and the head of the MP Administration. The military police, by virtue of the Law on Defence of 1993, was excluded from the structure of the armed forces and fell under the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacevic, follow my example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you prepared your report. Did you do the typewriting yourself, or did you deliver it handwritten?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give a printed-out copy to the Defence, or did you give an electronic version to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An electronic version, and the diagrams were on paper, and they were later introduced into the report. I mean the diagrams Mr. Russo inquired about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The layout of the report, that is, division in paragraphs, subparagraphs, et cetera, headers, footers, did you choose your own layout, or was that -- or was it later re-done -- done again by others?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all my work, only at the end the paragraph were enumerated, 1, 2, 3, and so on. That was the only addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Footers and headers were as you had created them, or were you given a certain format?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all mine. Mr. Kay gave me the general structure that I should follow, stipulating that I was free to work on it further to find the best structure that I saw fit. This was followed through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you specifically about headers and footers, whether you created them yourself, and were you given any instructions in this respect, or use footers, or say that, It should be page this out of so many? Or did you just find yourself the format and the layout?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written many books and articles in my life. Therefore, when I start to write something, I do it myself, then I re-read, go back, put in things that I think are missing, put in headers, et cetera. I did it all myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did it all yourself. Now, looking at the copy as it has been presented to this Court in your own language -- has the witness a copy? Could we have a look at -- perhaps have the report, whatever page it is, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He has a hard copy in front of him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the layout changed after you had delivered it, as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was changed, only the paragraphs were numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the line numbering, is that something you put into your draft? Because we have a copy in which every page the lines are numbered from 1 up to, well, up to over 40.

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then have a look at the copy you have to see -- to compare whether we are really looking at the same document? Could you just -- whatever page, one page, Croatian version, so that I can have a look at it. At the left, you see that all the lines of the pages are numbered, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, up to -- depending on the number of lines. Did you put this line numbering in there as well yourself?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was done subsequently. So someone has worked on the document. Was there anything else that -- in the layout that was changed, apart from this line numbering? Looking at the headers at the top of the page, I see "-40-B/C/S." That is what you put in there?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that part. This was according to the Rules of this Tribunal, in terms of what an expert report should contain. I asked for these designations to be entered, stating on what list that document can be found as evidence or on any of the lists, be it on the OTP or Defence sides. Nothing was changed in relation to what I had handed over. I only see that now they have numbered the lines, but not a single word was changed in relation to what I had written; only the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More specifically, looking at the header which you find at -- so not the numbers, but where it reads "IC-40-B/C/S," is that what you had put in this document?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not enter that, and also the line numbering was not done by me. I was told, though, that they would do that, before handing it over to the Tribunal on the 24th of July, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, at the footer, "Pero Kovacevic, strucni izvjestaj svjedoka," is that what you put in there or --

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was there from the start. When one is writing such a piece of work, one needs to have the correct pagination and those other things that one needs to have to prevent any additional insertion of pages or deletion of pages. This is a measure of prevention when compiling a piece of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's not what you were instructed to do, but you did it on your own?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on my own initiative. You can also find that in the many rules of intelligence services or in the minutes of parliamentary sessions. There are clear standards in terms of what should be contained in each page before such fora. This also applies to Master theses, expert articles, books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The cover page, the first page of your report, the layout of that, are you the intellectual author of that? So not the cover page in English, but the cover page saying "Page 1 out of 113," is the layout -- is that what you have chosen as a layout for the cover page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He's looking at a different page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking for the -- where it reads at the bottom "Sdr 1 od 130," that page which started "Izvjestaj Za Zlucaj [phoen] IT0690." That's the layout you have chosen for this page?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first page corresponds to other expert reports which I saw had been produced for the needs of this Tribunal. When I was constructing the first page, I followed the layout of Mr. Theunens. I looked at his cover page and the way he organised his expert report, in terms of layout -- layout and technical approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you just see Mr. Theunens' report, or did you use other expert reports as well to -- for choosing this layout?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first page is based on the expert report by Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you these questions because there is a striking similarity in the layout of the report of Mr. Feldi compared to yours. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the same. My title is different from his, and I never saw his expert report. In any case, I'm positive that the title is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about the layout rather than about the title. Of course, I wouldn't expect you to present a report under the same title. I'm just thinking in terms of layout on footnotes, headers, cover pages. Have you any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a comment. This was created the way I've explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Russo, have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know that I went beyond the time. Let's -- I'm stealing a bit of time, but I'll let you -- I'll take the blame for the Trial Chamber that follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I suppose Your Honour caused it because it arises from Your Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've been asked several questions about the pages of your report, the lines, what it looks like. Have you read your report?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. I wrote it myself, and I read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Has anyone inserted anything in your report that shouldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: PERO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not have signed it if anything was added to it. My report is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kovacevic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming your long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Thank you for coming. We'll adjourn, and we'll resume on Monday, the 28th of September, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
